# Rigveda Samhita — Volume 2
## English Translation of Sayana's Bhashya and Kannada Commentary (H. P. Venkata Rao)

**Source:** Sri Jayachamarajendra Vedaratnamala series, Volume 2. First Ashtaka, First Adhyaya, First Mandala, Suktas 3–9. Translated with exhaustive critical notes by Asthana Mahavidwan H. P. Venkata Rao, Editor. Printed at Sri Chamundeswari Electric Press, Clock Tower Square, Mysore, 1949. Published by permission of His Highness Sri Jayachamarajendra Wadiyar Bahadur, Maharaja of Mysore.

**Continuity note:** This is the direct continuation of Volume 1 (which covered the Purvapithika/Bhumika front matter in full, and Suktas 1–2 of Mandala 1). Volume 2 covers Suktas 3 through 9 of the same Adhyaya.

## Translator's Preface (ಪೀಠಿಕೆ)

**It has been about two years since the first part of the Rigveda — with Sayana's commentary and the Kannada translation — was completed.** The second part is now ready. Delays arose from insufficient printing facilities and other unavoidable circumstances. **Through these two parts together, only one Adhyaya out of the [64] Adhyayas of the Rigveda Samhita has been completed.** There is a wish to complete the remaining 63 Adhyayas as speedily as possible — with God's grace, perhaps within another 2–4 years. For readers' convenience, each future installment is planned to run to roughly 400 pages, which should both roughly halve the price of each part and let later installments reach readers more quickly.

**As stated before, although the meaning-translation follows Sayana's commentary, we have also incorporated, where contextually appropriate, a critical examination of the views of other ancient commentators and of Western scholars.** No one, in any language, has previously attempted so extensive a critical meaning-translation of the Rigveda. It is regrettable that earlier attempts at careful translations in Hindi, Marathi, and other languages were begun but could not even complete a single Adhyaya before being abandoned. The encouragement and esteem shown by many scholars and well-wishers — some writing letters of congratulation urging that this undertaking be completed however difficult it proves — has been especially heartening.

**A word on how this book's material is laid out:** ordinary readers who do not know Sanskrit can grasp the main sense from the Bhavartha (overall sense) alone. Those with some Sanskrit can read the Pratipadartha (word-meaning) and the English translation. Those wishing to study the Veda critically can, by also reading the special topics and grammar sections, grasp everything relevant. **Some feel the grammar portion is excessive — but only the grammar already present within Sayana's own commentary has been translated into Kannada.** Since grammar matters greatly for Vedic interpretation, it has been treated somewhat fully at the start, though it will gradually diminish in later parts. Episodes, earlier histories, and matters needing clarification are explained with the help of the other Vedas and works such as the Puranas, as occasion requires.

**Everyone agrees that critical examination of Vedic meaning is an extremely profound matter** — which is precisely why even ordinary people, and even Sanskrit-knowing scholars, hesitate to engage with it. Yet this has not stopped renowned scholars, ancient and modern, from attempting it. The Vedas — the Rigveda Samhita especially — being extremely ancient, much of their vocabulary, style, and subject matter is no longer current today. **Since Vedic words had already fallen out of common usage some 3,000 years ago, the sage Yaska composed, in that very era, the great treatise called the Nirukta** to explain their meanings; every subsequent commentator has taken the Nirukta as his foundation. Since a great many Vedic words are not current in later Sanskrit, their forms must be derived through grammar and meanings fitted accordingly — **but whether such grammatically-derived meanings truly match the intent of the ancient rishis remains genuinely open to doubt**, and despite extensive debate, nothing has ever been definitively settled, nor is it likely to be. Still, just as the Rigveda is the foundation among the Vedas, there is no doubt that Yaska's Nirukta is the foundation of all Vedic commentary.

**Publishing such an ancient, profound, vast Samhita — foundational to all branches of knowledge — in simple Kannada with critical commentary, is no easy task.** It is undertaken so that all people, learned and simple alike, might grow in knowledge and become worthy of divine grace. The generous patronage of His Highness Sri Jayachamarajendra Odeyar Bahadur, G.C.B., G.C.S.I. — ruler of the Karnataka throne, patron of Vedic learning, himself a scholar, beloved of his subjects, devoted to Shiva — in supporting this resource-intensive publication is the good fortune of the Karnataka people. The translator closes with a prayer for the Maharaja, his family (including the Princess named after the Gayatri mantra, foremost among Vedic mantras), and all his subjects, that the Lord of the Universe — himself the embodiment of the Veda — grant them worldly prosperity and, doubly, transcendent spiritual knowledge.

*Mysore. [Virodhi-nama Samvatsara, Jyeshtha Bahula Saptami, Friday] 17 June 1949.*

*Translator: H. P. Venkata Rao, Asthana Mahavidwan.*

# Part II — Saṃhitā Text, Continued

### Page 1

**॥ Śrī Mahāgaṇādhipataye Namaḥ ॥**

> वागीशाद्याः सुमनसः सर्वार्थानामुपक्रमे । यं नत्वा कृतकृत्याः स्युस्तं नमामि गजाननम् ॥
> यस्य निःश्वसितं वेदा यो वेदेभ्योऽखिलं जगत् । निर्ममे तमहं वन्दे विद्यातीर्थमहेश्वरम् ॥
> वेदः शिवः शिवो वेदो वेदाध्याया सदाशिवः । तस्मात्सर्वप्रयत्नेन वेदमेव सदा जपेत् ॥
>
> *(The same three invocatory verses that open Volume 1 — to Gaṇapati, Sarasvatī, and the Veda itself as the breath of the Supreme Lord.)*

**॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya-sahitā Ṛgveda Saṃhitā — Bhāga 2 ॥**

**Having begun to set down the first of the four Vedas — the Rigveda, which takes the very form of the Supreme Lord's own breath — together with Sayana's commentary, Kannada translation and explanation, and much other useful material, we explained at length, in the first part, the Rigveda's Purva-pithika (preliminary introduction), Sayana's Bhashya-Bhumika, and, within the Samhita-portion's first Mandala, the meaning-translation of the first two suktas, "Agnim īḷe purohitam" and "Vāyav ā yāhi darśata." We now begin, in this second part, the meaning-translation of the third sukta, "Aśvinā yajña-vīriṇiṣaḥ."**

**The Rigveda Samhita contains 1,028 suktas in total, composed by many rishis who served as their seers.** This Samhita, comprising these 1,028 suktas, is divided into ten Mandalas; each Mandala is further divided into several Anuvakas; each Anuvaka...

### Page 2 — [Maṇḍala 1, Adhyāya 1, Sūkta 3]

**...[Mandalas] are divided into suktas. The first Mandala has 191 suktas, divided into 24 Anuvakas.** Their arrangement is given in the following table, listing each Anuvaka's sukta-range, sukta-count, and cumulative count of mantras:

| Anuvaka | Sukta range | Suktas in this Anuvaka | Cumulative mantras |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1–9 | 9 | 70 |
| 2 | 10–19 *(approx.)* | ... | ... |
| *(remaining 22 rows)* | | | |
| **Total** | **1–191** | **191** | *(a four-digit total, approx. 2000+)* |

*(This table runs to 24 rows of small Kannada numerals at this scan's resolution; the first row is given with reasonable confidence, but the remaining rows are not transcribed individually here to avoid asserting precise figures that cannot be verified reliably at this resolution. The prose below confirms the totals that matter: 191 suktas across 24 Anuvakas in Mandala 1.)*

**These suktas do not all treat of a single deity.** They contain hymns addressed to many deities — Agni, Indra, Vayu, and others. The rishis (the mantra-seers, those who "saw" or composed the mantras) are likewise numerous. Among them are Vishvamitra, Vasishtha, Vamadeva...

### Page 3

**...Gotama, Bharadvaja and other members of the seven great rishi-lineages, their descendants, and the many further rishis belonging to their disciple-lines.** The names of the Rigveda's rishis, together with the suktas and mantra-counts each composed, have already been given in Volume 1 (pages 191–205). Among meters too, there are many varieties and sub-varieties — Gayatri, Trishtubh, Jagati, and others. **The Rigveda's 1,028 suktas, composed in all these varied meters, may be organized in three different ways:**

**1. Ṛṣi-krama (ordering by rishi)** — grouping the suktas composed by a given principal rishi and his descendants into a single section or Mandala. **Mandalas 2 through 7 of the Rigveda (six Mandalas in total) are arranged this way.**

**2. Devatā-krama (ordering by deity)** — grouping together the mantras or suktas that praise a given deity. That is: one group for Agni-related suktas, another for Indra-related suktas, and so on. **This ordering is followed in the Rigveda's ninth Mandala, where every single sukta shares the same deity — Soma — with no other deity appearing at all; only the rishis and meters differ from sukta to sukta.**

**3. Chandaḥ-krama (ordering by meter)** — grouping together mantras (or suktas) that share a single meter: all Gayatri-meter mantras in one group, all Trishtubh-meter mantras in another, and so on for every meter. **This third ordering is not found to be followed consistently anywhere, and so is not actually used in the Rigveda.**

**Beyond these, since the suktas grouped under the first scheme (Rishi-krama) include many quite short ones, gathering all these together into a single Mandala forms yet another arrangement — found in Mandalas 1 and 10.**

**In Mandala 1, there is, broadly speaking, one rishi for roughly every hundred mantras** (the exact count varies somewhat). For example: in the first Mandala, mantras 1 through 102 belong to **Madhucchandas Vaishvamitra**; mantras 101 [sic] through 140 to **Medhatithi Kanva**; and mantras 141 through 160 to **Ajigarti Shunahshepa**. **This is likely why the rishis of this first Mandala are called "Śatarcinaḥ"** ("those who composed a hundred riks each").

**Mandala 10 does not follow this scheme either.** This Mandala contains many quite short suktas (kṣudra-suktas) composed both by members of the seven rishi-lineages and by rishis outside them...

### Page 4

**...The "deities" here include not only principal ones like Agni and Indra, but also lesser deities, and even hymns of praise to inanimate things such as Night (Rātrī) and Faith (Śraddhā). Such a wide variety of suktas is found in the tenth Mandala.**

**A given sukta may contain anywhere from one mantra to any number.** Generally, mantras addressed to a single deity are counted as one sukta. Before reciting any Vedic mantra, one must first state its rishi, deity, and meter — only then the mantra itself. A single mantra may have its own rishi, or many suktas may share one rishi. **Apart from Mandalas 1, 9, and 10, each of the remaining Mandalas belongs to a single group of rishis.**

**A definite sequence governs how the suktas are arranged.** Within a Mandala, among the suktas belonging to a given rishi, those connected with Agni come first. Among these, Gayatri-meter suktas come first, followed by Trishtubh, Jagati, and other meters. Within each such group, the shortest suktas (3, 4, 5, 6 mantras) come first, with progressively longer ones following. **Once the Agni-deity suktas are exhausted, the Indra-deity suktas begin, arranged the same way; after these come suktas for other deities — the Vishvadevas, Ushas, and so on.** Many suktas have multiple rishis, deities, or meters within themselves; such suktas occur here and there throughout. After all of a given rishi's suktas are exhausted, the suktas of the next rishi connected with that Mandala begin, following this same sequence. **Only in the ninth Mandala — where every sukta shares the single deity Soma — is the meter-sequence (Gayatri first, etc.) governed instead by sukta-length.**

**Suktas generally address a single deity, but a sukta may sometimes have multiple deities:** each mantra within it may have its own separate deity, or even a single mantra may have two deities together. **For example: the second sukta of Mandala 1 has 9 mantras, with Vāyu, then Indra-Vāyu, then Mitrā-Varuṇā as deities in groups of three.** In the same Mandala, the sixth sukta's ten mantras have Indra as deity for the first three; of the rest, the eighth and ninth have the Maruts, and the remaining mantras have, one each in sequence, Marut, Indra-Marut, Marut, and Indra-Marut as deities. **The fourteenth sukta's twelve mantras** (a special case — "this sukta is addressed to the Vishve...")

### Page 5

**...["devaiḥ sahito agni-devatā"] — Agni accompanied by the Vishvadevas is the deity here.** In the ninth mantra of the thirteenth sukta, there are three deities together: Sarasvati, Ila, and Bharati. Many such examples exist, but generally a sukta has a single deity.

**The deities appearing with special prominence in the Rigveda are Agni, Indra, the Maruts, the Vishvadevas, the Ashvins, and Pavamana-Soma.** Among these, the greatest number of mantras concern Agni and Indra. **Taken as a whole, roughly a quarter of the entire Rigveda concerns Indra**; after Indra, the next-greatest share concerns Agni; then the other deities follow.

**A further distinctive feature appears across the Mandalas: apart from the eighth and ninth, each of the remaining eight Mandalas opens its first sukta with Agni.** The eighth Mandala instead opens with a mantra devoted to Indra. **The ninth Mandala alone is devoted throughout to a single deity — Pavamana-Soma** — and, unlike the other Mandalas, its rishis do not belong to one single group; rishis from other Mandalas appear here too. **The tenth Mandala's rishis likewise belong to many different groups, and its deities are correspondingly numerous.**

**Turning to our present topic: since Suktas 1 and 2 of the first Anuvaka have already been explained in Volume 1, we now begin the third sukta, "Aśvinā yajña-vīriṣaḥ," which closes this Anuvaka.**

**Before the meaning-translation, we first state this sukta's application (viniyoga):**

> अश्विनेति द्वादशर्चं तृतीयं सूक्तम् । तत्राश्विनस्तिस‍ृच प्रातरनुवाकस्याश्विने कृतौ विनियुक्ताः । कथं च सूत्रितम् । अथाश्विना एषो उषाः प्रातरिति चतस‍ृचाश्विनी यज्ञवीरिषः ॥ आ. ४-३-७ ॥
> *aśvineti dvādaśarcaṃ tṛtīyaṃ sūktam | tatrāśvinas tisṛca prātar-anuvākasyāśvine kṛtau viniyuktāḥ | kathaṃ ca sūtritam | athāśvina eṣo uṣāḥ prātar iti catasṛc āśvinī yajña-vīriṣaḥ || Ā. 4.3.7 ||*
> "'Aśvinā...' is the third sukta, comprising twelve [thirteen] riks. Of these, the three Ashvin-riks are applied in the Ashvin-portion of the Pratar-anuvaka. And thus it is stated in the Sutra: 'athāśvinā eṣo uṣāḥ prātar' — these four riks [together are] 'Āśvinī Yajña-vīriṣaḥ.'" (Āśvalāyana Sūtra 4.3.7)

**This sukta has 13 mantras, grouped into 4 Ṛcas** — a "Ṛca" here meaning a group of three mantras. **The first Ṛca (mantras 1–3) has the Ashvin deities; the second Ṛca (mantras 4–6) has Indra; the third Ṛca (mantras 7–9) has the Vishvadevas; and the fourth Ṛca (mantras 10–12) has Sarasvati as deity.**

**We have already given, in Volume 1 (pages 667–669), a concise account of the Agnishtoma-yaga.** In the Agnishtoma, the day on which Soma-juice is pressed is called "Sutya-dina"; since suktas recited as Stotra and Shastra are also rehearsed at the time of pressing, this day is also called "Stutya-dina." On that day, in the early morning — that is...

### Page 6

**...before sunrise, after the previous night's midnight has passed, and before the birds' morning calls begin, the Hotṛ must finish reciting the mantras called the Prātar-anuvāka.** This Prātar-anuvāka comprises three portions: the Āgneya-kratu (Riks connected with Agni), the Auṣasya-kratu, and the Āśvina-kratu. Each portion must contain numerous mantras spanning the seven meters — Gāyatrī, Anuṣṭubh, Triṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, Uṣṇik, Jagatī, and Paṅkti.

**After the Prātar-anuvāka is recited, the rite called "Prātaḥ-savana" takes place.** "Savana" means crushing the Soma creeper with stones (grāvāṇa) and extracting its juice. This occurs at three times: morning extraction is "Prātaḥ-savana"; midday extraction, "Mādhyandina-savana"; evening extraction, "Tṛtīya-savana."

**Across these three Savanas, twelve Stotras and twelve Shastra-mantras must be recited in total.** "Stotra" means Riks fit for chanting (sāmagāna), sung by the Udgātṛ; as soon as he finishes each Stotra, the Hotṛ, in response, recites the corresponding Shastra-mantras (Rigveda Riks). "Shastra" means a Rigveda mantra recited melodiously but without being sung. **These Shastra-mantras are recited by the Hotṛ and his assistant priests — the Maitrāvaruṇa, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsī, and Acchāvāka.** The full arrangement of these mantras across the three Savanas in the Agnishtoma's Prātar-anuvāka is given below:

**1. Prātaḥ-savana**

| Stotra-mantras | Shastra-mantras |
|---|---|
| 1. Bahiṣpavamāna-stotra | 1. Ājya-śastra |
| 2. Ājya-stotras | 2. Praüga-śastra |
| *(these recited by the Hotṛ)* | |
| 3. " | 3. Ājya-śastras |
| 4. " | 4. " |
| 5. " | 5. " |

*(The first two Stotras are sung by the Udgātṛ; the latter three Shastras are recited by the Hotṛ's assistant priests — Maitrāvaruṇa, Brāhmaṇācchaṃsī, and Acchāvāka.)*

**The Bhashyakara's own glosses confirm this:** "Ājyaiḥ stuvate" — the Udgātṛ chants the Ajya-stotra mantras (in the morning pressing); "Pṛṣṭhaiḥ stuvate" — the Udgātṛ chants the Prishtha-stotra mantras (in the midday pressing); "pralugaṃ śaṃsati" — the Hotṛ recites the Pralugat-shastra mantras (in the morning pressing); "niṣkevalyaṃ śaṃsati" — the Hotṛ recites the Nishkevalya-shastra mantras (in the midday pressing). That is: as soon as the Udgātṛ finishes the Ajya-stotras in the morning pressing, the Hotṛ, in response, recites the Pralugat-shastra mantras; likewise for Prishtha-stotra and Nishkevalya-shastra in the midday pressing, and so on.

**During the recitation of the Prātar-anuvāka, the sukta "Agnimīḷe" is recited — its application was already stated earlier (Volume 1), as was the application of the second sukta "Vāyav ā yāhi," a nine-mantra sukta.** We now come to the third sukta, "Aśvinā yajña-vīriṣaḥ," a twelve-mantra sukta, which the Hotṛ must recite during the Pralugat-shastra portion. **The sequence of the Pralugat-shastra mantras runs as follows: Vāyu, Indra-Vāyu, Mitrā-Varuṇā, Aśvin, Indra, Viśvedevāḥ, Sarasvatī** — mantras praising these seven deities in turn, each deity addressed by three mantras (called a "Ṛca"). Within the sukta "Vāyav ā yāhi"...

### Page 8

**...of the nine mantras [in "Vāyav ā yāhi"]: the first three concern Vāyu; four through six concern Indra-Vāyu; seven through nine concern Mitrā-Varuṇā. In the sukta "Aśvinā yajña-vīriṣaḥ" that follows: mantras one through three concern the Ashvins; four through six, Indra; seven through nine, the Vishvadevas; and nine through twelve, Sarasvatī.** Together, these two suktas thus form seven groups of three mantras (21 mantras total), addressed to seven deities' Shastra-mantras. **The Hotṛ must recite these during the second [sukta's] Pralugat-shastra recitation in the morning pressing, immediately after the Udgātṛ sings the Ajya-stotras.** This is the application of both the second and third suktas.

**This sequence is confirmed in the Aitareya Brahmana, in the section beginning "gṛho'laṃ" (Aitareya Brahmana 3.1), and by Ashvalayana in his own Shrauta-sutra, in the section "stotram agre śastrāt" (Ashvalayana Sutra 5.10).** The Anukramanika states it thus:

> वायो वायव्यमिन्द्रवायवमित्रावरुणाऋचा अश्विना द्वादशाश्वैन्द्रैश्वदेवसारस्वासृचा सप्तृचा प्रलुगदेवता ।
> *(this compressed index-entry, confirming the seven-deity structure just described, remains a genuinely dense best-effort reading)*

**That is: in "Vāyav ā yāhi," each group of three mantras addresses one deity — Vāyu, Indra-Vāyu, Mitrā-Varuṇā — three deities in all; and in "Aśvinā yajña-vīriṣaḥ," similarly, each group of three addresses Aśvinā, Indra, Viśvedevāḥ, Sarasvatī — four further deities. Together, these seven deities bear the name "Pralugat-devatāḥ." This is this sukta's full application-sequence.**

> अश्विना । यज्वरीः । इषः । द्रवत्पाणी इति द्रवत्पाणी । शुभः । पती इति ।

**॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥**

> हे अश्विना युवामिमे शनिर्लक्षणान्नानि चनस्यतम् । इच्छतम् । भुंजाथामित्यर्थः । यद्वापि चनिशब्दोऽन्नवाचे तथापीषेत्यनेन सह नास्ति पुनरुक्तिदोषः । इच्छामुपलक्षयितुं प्रयुक्तत्वात् । वक्तव्यमुच्यते । समूलकाशं कृषतीत्यादौ यथा पुनरुक्तभावस्तत् । कीदृशीरिषः । यज्वरीः । यागनिष्पादिकाः । कीदृशावश्विना । द्रवत्पाणी । शीघ्रग्रहणाय प्रवद्भ्यां धावद्भ्यां पाणिभ्यामुपेतौ । शुभस्पती । शोभनस्य कर्मणः पालकौ । पुरुभुजा । विस्तीर्णभुजौ बहुभोजौ ।
> *he aśvinā yuvām ime śanir-lakṣaṇānnāni canasyatam | icchatam | bhuñjāthām ity arthaḥ | yadvāpi cani-śabdo'nna-vāce tathāpīṣety anena saha nāsti punarukti-doṣaḥ | icchām upalakṣayituṃ prayuktatvāt | vaktavyam ucyate | samūla-kāśaṃ kṛṣatīty ādau yathā punarukta-bhāvas tat | kīdṛśīr iṣaḥ | yajvarīḥ | yāga-niṣpādikāḥ | kīdṛśāv aśvinā | dravat-pāṇī | śīghra-grahaṇāya pravadbhyāṃ dhāvadbhyāṃ pāṇibhyām upetau | śubhas patī | śobhanasya karmaṇaḥ pālakau | purubhujā | vistīrṇa-bhujau bahu-bhojau |*

**Translation:** "O Ashvins! You two desire ('canasyatam') these foods marked by swiftness — the sense being, 'may you two partake.' Even though the word 'cani' itself means 'food,' joining it with 'iṣa' (also 'food') is not a fault of redundancy, since here it is used specifically to convey the sense of 'desiring'; this needs to be stated, [just as there is no redundancy] in expressions like 'samūla-kāśaṃ kṛṣati' [a comparable grammatical construction]. What kind of foods? 'Yajvarīḥ' — those that bring the sacrifice to completion. What kind of pair are the Ashvins? 'Dravat-pāṇī' — possessing hands that move quick and swift, for grasping things rapidly. 'Śubhas-patī' — protectors of auspicious action. 'Purubhujā' — broad-armed, enjoying much..."

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

O Ashvin deities! You are protectors who ensure that auspicious undertakings proceed without obstacle. Your arms reach to your knees, your shoulders are exceedingly broad — or, you are those who eat abundantly. Therefore, come now quickly, hands outstretched, to partake of the oblation we have prepared in this yajna, and eat this food.

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> O Asvins, you are cherishers of good deeds, your arms are long (or you are great eaters). You desire the sacrificial food with outstretched hands.

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥**

**The Ashvin deities are two in number.** One is customarily called "Dasra" and the other "Nāsatya," though these words are often found used to address both together. **Regarding their origin, the Puranas preserve a legend:** Sañjñā-devī, wife of Sūrya the Sun, having grown dissatisfied with him for some reason, went into the forest and took the form of a mare to perform austerities there. When Sūrya learned of this, he too took the form of a horse and joined her there for a time; from this union, it is said, the Ashvin deities were born. **The Rigveda contains many suktas concerning them, deeply dignified in tone and full of praise for their other qualities and heroic deeds.** The Yajurveda states, "aśvinau vai devānāṃ bhiṣajau" — that these two are the physicians of the gods.

**In connection with a rishi named Ṛjrāśva:** while grazing his father's goats in a forest, the Ashvin deities came to him in the form of wolves (vṛka), and he gave them a hundred goats as food. When his father learned of this, in great anger he put out his son's eyes and blinded him. Rjrashva then prayed to the Ashvins; pleased by his hymn, they restored his sight and blessed him — this is related in the 116th sukta of this Mandala. **Many further legends and heroic deeds of these deities are recounted in Suktas 118–120 and elsewhere.**

**In the Rigveda, certain fixed words are consistently used when praising particular deities.** In praising Agni: words such as "kavi" (the wise one), "hotṛ" (priest), "gṛhapati" (householder), and others. Concerning Indra: "śatakratu" (of a hundred powers), "vṛtraghna" (slayer of Vritra), "puruhūta" (much-invoked), "citrabhānu" (of brilliant radiance), and others. For the Ashvins...

### Page 12

**...concerning these deities, words such as "Nāsatyā," "Śubhaspatī," "Narā," "Purubhujā," and "Rathe-vantau" are used.** Since all the rishis use many such words in connection with these very deities, it is clear these words must carry some specific, fixed sense beyond what now merely occurs to us or has become conventional. It is genuinely difficult now to say precisely in what sense the rishis originally intended them. **Even where we construct a plausible sense — through grammar or component-meaning analysis — whether that sense truly matches the ancient rishis' own intent remains open to doubt**, since this textual tradition is so ancient that these words no longer carry their original meanings; their senses differ in modern Sanskrit, so our commentarial meanings cannot be asserted as certainly correct.

**The word "Aśvinā" (or "Aśvinau") appears in the Rigveda in three distinct accentual forms** — *aśvínā, áśvinā, aśvinā́*; *aśvínau, áśvinau, aśvinaú* — used in many different places. The first takes initial-udātta accent, the second is fully unaccented; both are customarily used when addressing the Ashvins directly (vocative). The third, with middle-syllable udātta, is used when expressing "of the Ashvins" or "the Ashvins" as object.

**Since "Aśvinā" functions as a proper name — denoting specific, fixed individuals — constructing an etymological (component) meaning for it is not strictly correct.** Still, the authors of the Vedārtha-yatna explain it as: "aśvaḥ asya āpta iti aśvī, tau aśvinā" — "those who possess a horse" or "those who ride a horse." **But this sense finds no real support in the Rigveda** — in many mantras the Ashvins are addressed as seated upon a chariot, never as riding horseback; their view therefore does not seem fitting. **It seems more reasonable to suppose that the Ashvins came to be called "Aśvinā" because they were born from Sūrya and Sañjñā-devī while both were in horse-form** — connecting the name directly to the origin-legend already given. Both "Aśvinā" and "Aśvinau" are dual forms, used in the nominative and accusative according to context.

**"Yajvarī"** — this word occurs in only two mantras of the entire Rigveda Samhita. In this mantra too...

### Page 13

> प्रातेयुर्जं नासत्याधि तिष्ठः प्रातर्यानाणं मधुवाहनं रथम् । विश्वे येन गच्छथो यज्वरीर्नरा कीरेश्चिद्ध्यश्च होत्रमन्तमश्विना ॥ (ऋ. सं. १०-४०-३)
> *(this citation confirms "yajvarī" occurring in its only other appearance in the Rigveda — the cited verse-number here is taken as given in the source)*

**This word is found in only this one other mantra. In both places it carries the same meaning — there is nothing further special to note.**

**"Iṣaḥ"** — the word "iṣa" means food, nourishment. This word's form occurs both as initial-udātta ("íṣaḥ") and final-udātta ("iṣáḥ").

**"Dravat-pāṇī"** — this word occurs only in this one mantra within the entire Rigveda Samhita. Its fourth-case plural form, "dravat-pāṇibhyaḥ," occurs only in:

> हिरण्ययेन रथेन द्रवत्पाणिभिरश्विना । धीजवना नासत्या ॥ (ऋ. सं. ८-५-८)
> *hiraṇyayena rathena dravat-pāṇibhir aśvinā | dhījavanā nāsatyā ||* (Rigveda Samhita 8.5.8)

**— nowhere else does this word appear. Its meaning, per Sayana, is "those who have loosened or outstretched their hands."** For this sense to fit both mantras consistently, in this second citation — where "dravat-pāṇibhiḥ" qualifies the chariot-horses — the word must instead be read as "with swiftly-moving feet/hooves," i.e., "by horse." **The word "pāṇi" must therefore be understood as capable of indicating two senses here: hands, and feet (hooves).**

**"Śubhas-patī"** — the Bhashya explains "śubhaḥ" and "patī" together as "those who bring about auspicious deeds." **Skandasvāmī and Veṅkaṭanātha explain these words as "udakeśvarau"** — "lords of water" — taking "śubha" to mean "waters" in their view. **The Vedārtha-yatna authors render it "Lords of prosperity."** **Western scholars — Grassmann, Ludwig, Geldner, Monier Williams, Griffith — endorse "Lords of Splendour,"** following the root "śubh/śumbh" (to shine). This dual-form word occurs in the Rigveda at: 1.3.1; 1.34.4; 1.47.2; 1.120.6; 8.2.4; 8.7.2; 8.8.8; 10.40.7; 10.40.12; 10.40.13; 10.64.4; 10.110.4; 8.19.3; 8.34.3. **In the last two of these it concerns Indra-Varuna; in every other instance it concerns the Ashvins.** Similarly, words such as "Śavasas-patī" and "Danus-patī" are used of other deities, but never of the Ashvins. Sāyaṇācārya, on the word "Śubhaspatī"...

### Page 14

**...glosses the word differently in different places — in one or two instances, "śubha" is glossed as "splendor, radiance" instead. The precise meaning of this word therefore remains genuinely unsettled.**

**Furthermore, in the Rigveda, the word "patī" serves as the latter member of several compounds:**

- **Sadas-patī** (Rigveda Samhita 1.18.6)
- **Go-patī** (Rigveda Samhita 4.1.1)
- **Dam-patī** (Rigveda Samhita 4.3.2; 7.20.5; 10.40.5; 10.51.3; 10.71.1; 10.13.5)
- **Nṛ-patī** (Rigveda Samhita 6.67.1; 6.67.4)
- **Mada-patī** (Rigveda Samhita 4.79.2)
- **Vana-patī** (Rigveda Samhita 1.64.4)
- **Śacī-patī** (Rigveda Samhita 4.67.4)
- **Sapta-patī** (Rigveda Samhita 1.66.2; 1.10.4; 10.67.2)
- **Sindhu-patī** (Rigveda Samhita 4.67.2)
- **Svaḥ-patī** (Rigveda Samhita 4.1.1)

**"Purubhujā"** — a dual-ending word, occurring in ten mantras (Rigveda Samhita 1.3.1; 1.118.1; 1.118.13; 4.43.1; 4.51.1; 8.5.3; 8.10.8; 8.8.21; 8.86.1). In this mantra it takes initial-udātta accent; elsewhere it is fully unaccented — fitting, since fully-unaccented proper-name words generally indicate the vocative. **Its meaning varies across occurrences:**

> अजोऽपीन्वासत्या करा वां महे यामन्पुरुभुजा पुरंधिः ।

**Here "purubhujā" means "protector of many" — one who protects many people.**

> उतो कविं पुरुभुजा युवं ह कृशमाणमकृणुतं विचक्षे ।
> *uto kaviṃ purubhujā yuvaṃ ha kṛśamāṇam akṛṇutaṃ vicakṣe |* (Rigveda Samhita 1.118.6)

**Here "Purubhujā" means "great-armed," "possessing abundant arms/hands."**

---

**"Canasyatam"** — raises a genuine question: since this dual-verb itself means "partake of food," and it governs "iṣaḥ" (food, in the form of oblation), doesn't stating "food" twice create a redundancy fault? **The commentator answers that such apparently-redundant pairings are a well-established convention occurring in many contexts**, citing as an illustrative (non-Vedic) parallel the phrase "samūla-kāśaṃ kṛṣati." **Such redundancy-adjacent word-pairs do occur here and there within the Veda itself; a few are given below as examples —**

### Page 16

> यो अश्वानां यो गवां गोपतिर्वृषा य आरितः कर्मणिकर्मणि स्थिरः ।
> *yo aśvānāṃ yo gavāṃ go-patir vṛṣā ya āritaḥ karmaṇi-karmaṇi sthiraḥ |* (Rigveda Samhita 1.101.5)

> इहेन्द्राग्नी उप श्रयं तयोरित्था मुमुच्यासि । ता सोमं सोमपातमा ॥
> *ihendrāgnī upa śrayaṃ tayor itthā mumucyāsi | tā somaṃ somapātamā ||* (Rigveda Samhita 8.38.4)

> द्विषणोदा द्विषणस्युरस्य द्विषणोदाः सनरस्य यंसत् ।
> *dviṣaṇodā dviṣaṇasyuras ya dviṣaṇodāḥ sanarasya yaṃsat |* (Rigveda Samhita 1.36.1)

**These mantras, with phrases like "gavāṃ go-patiḥ" (the cow-protector of cows), "somaṃ soma-pātamā" (the soma-drinkers of soma), and "dviṣaṇodā dviṣaṇasya," confirm that this kind of apparent redundancy is a genuine, established feature of Vedic diction.**

**॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥**

*(The grammatical derivation for this sukta's opening verse — covering "aśvinā" as a vocative-adjacent form (per Phit-sutra 1.1.28), "yajvarī" analyzed via the root meaning "to accomplish the sacrifice," "iṣaḥ" and its accent-variants, "dravat-pāṇī" as a compound of "dravat" (running/swift) and "pāṇi" (hand/foot), "śubhas-patī" with its accent-retention rule, and "canasyatam" as a denominative verb formed from "canas" — proceeds here in the same dense sutra-citation register used throughout this work. Given its density, it is characterized here rather than transcribed line by line, consistent with standing practice; none of it alters the senses already established above in the Bhāṣya, Pratipadārtha, and Viśeṣārtha sections for this verse.)*

### Page 18 — Sūkta 3, The Second Mantra

*(The bulk of this page continues the Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya's grammatical analysis of "purudaṃsasā," "dhiṣṇyā," "vanatam," and "giraḥ" in the established dense register — covering compound-formation, accent-retention rules, and cross-references to related forms elsewhere in the Rigveda. Characterized here rather than transcribed line-by-line, consistent with standing practice.)*

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**पुरुदंससा (purudaṃsasā)** — endowed with many deeds, that is, performers of many works | **नरा (narā)** — leaders of people, or guides | **धिष्ण्या (dhiṣṇyā)** — wise | **अश्विना (aśvinā)** — O Ashvin deities! (you two) | **शवीरया (śavīrayā)** — unimpeded, unobstructed | **धिया (dhiyā)** — with that understanding | **गिरः (giraḥ)** — the words of praise we offer | **वनतम् (vanatam)** — accept.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

O Ashvin deities! You are those who perform many deeds — heroic undertakings; you are guides for people, exceedingly wise, and full of courage. Being such, with your unimpeded understanding, graciously and attentively accept the hymns of praise we now offer in these words.

### Page 20

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> O Aswins, performers of mighty deeds, leaders of men, endowed with fortitude, accept our praises with unaverted (loving) mind.

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥**

**The three mantras in this sukta expounding the Ashvin deities are all genuinely difficult.** Many commentators, following grammatical derivation, have constructed component-based meanings for these words and presented them as though settled by ordinary reasoning. **But for many Rigveda words, such component-based construction simply does not yield a fitting sense.** There is good reason to think that the meanings now conventional for these words in present-day Sanskrit were not current in the Vedic period, and that these words once carried their own distinct senses. **At that time, grammar itself had not yet been composed.** There is no doubt that the great sage Pāṇini composed his grammar taking Vedic vocabulary itself as his foundational basis, nor that Pāṇini's grammar is authoritative for explaining the derivation of words now current in Sanskrit — **but many Vedic words simply do not fall under these later grammatical rules.** For example, a single word is sometimes expressed in different forms while keeping the same meaning. **Language came first; grammar was composed afterward, by following the patterns already present in language — never the reverse.** Therefore, even where we construct, through component-meaning analysis, some fitting sense for a Vedic word, **to claim that the ancient rishis actually used that word in precisely that derived sense would be a genuine act of overreach.**

---

**"Purudaṃsasā"** — this word occurs in four mantras of the Rigveda. In this mantra it is initial-udātta; in Rigveda Samhita 8.5.10 and 8.22.3 it is fully unaccented (confirming, as already noted, that fully-unaccented nominative forms serve the vocative); in 8.26.1 it is middle-udātta. **Further forms of this word — "purudaṃsam" and "purudaṃsā" — occur in Rigveda Samhita 1.3.2 and 7.67.1; nowhere else.** The word comprises two separate elements, "puru" and "daṃsa." "Puru" means "much, abundant" — the same element already discussed in "purubhujā" above. **"Daṃsa" is listed among the words meaning "karma" (action, deed); hence the compound means "deed" or "work."** The Bhashyakara accordingly explains "purudaṃsā" as "bahu-karmāṇau" — "those possessing the capacity for many deeds."

### Page 21

**Veṅkaṭamādhava glosses this as "āścarya-bhūta-vividha-karmāṇau"** — those whose various deeds are a source of wonder. **Wilson explains it as "performers of marvelous or heroic deeds"; Grassmann and Ludwig, following Veṅkaṭamādhava's own reading, state "those who perform wondrous deeds."** Since Suktas 112, 114, 118, and 119 of this Mandala describe many heroic deeds of these deities, **Veṅkaṭamādhava's view appears correct.**

**"Narā"** — Sayana and Veṅkaṭamādhava explain this as "netārau" — leaders, guides; Skandasvāmī, as "those possessing human form." **Wilson expresses Sayana's meaning by "guides." Whitney renders "narah" with "manly," and Stevenson with "who assumes the human form"; Geldner, in his Der Rigveda, gives several meanings of this word.** Among these, Sayana's view seems most sound. Still, since "narā" is used specifically in contexts praising the Ashvin deities, it can confidently be said that the word carried some specific, fixed sense in its own time.

**"Śavīrayā"** — this word occurs in the Rigveda only here and in:

> अश्विनावश्वयाता यातं शवीरया । (ऋ. सं. १-४०-१?)

**— nowhere else. The Bhashyakara derives it from the root "śū" (to go) with the affix "vīra," giving "endowed with motion," that is, "possessing unimpeded power."** As a feminine noun in the fourth-case singular, it is treated as qualifying "dhiyā" (understanding). **Veṅkaṭamādhava explains it differently: "śu" means "swift," "īra" means "to go," hence "śavīra" means "swift-moving."** Alternatively, he connects it to "śava" (strength, listed among the Nighaṇṭu's strength-words), giving the sense "those who go swiftly to destroy the enemy's strength" or "those who hasten to the sacrificial altar to receive their share of the oblation" — on this reading, "śavīrayā" becomes instead a nominative dual form qualifying "Aśvinā" itself...

### Page 22

**...as stated. The Vedārtha-yatna authors and Western scholars explain "śavīra" as "Strong, Mighty, Powerful."**

**"Dhiyā"** — Sayana and Skandasvāmī explain this as "ādara-yuktayā buddhyā" — "with reverent understanding," reading it as an instrumental. Some Western scholars gloss "dhiyā" as "mind, thought, aim," connecting it to the verb "vanatam"; the Bhashyakara harmonizes it the same way. **But Veṅkaṭamādhava treats "dhiyā" instead as a qualifier of "dhiṣṇyā."** In many contexts "dhiyā" is used in the nominative, meaning "possessing intelligence."

**"Dhiṣṇyā"** — the Bhashyakara explains this as "dhārṣṭrya-yuktau" (possessing boldness) or "buddhimantau" (wise). **Skandasvāmī derives it: "Dhiṣaṇā" means speech; her offspring, or the word "dhī" (insight) in its own feminine form, yields "dhiṣṇyā" — "those exceedingly wise, capable of grasping every matter."** Sayana's gloss — "courageous, wise" — is endorsed by Wilson. **Grassmann renders it "free giving, willingly giving, willingly helping"; Geldner, "wise"; Ludwig, "praiseworthy."** By a different word-family connection (from the root "dhī," to think), other commentators explain "Dhiṣṇyā" as "those that kindle the thoughts" — those who inspire the mind or speech. This word is initial-udātta at Rigveda Samhita 1.3.3; 1.104.3; 3.47.1; and fully unaccented at 1.84.4; 1.102.1; 1.110.2; 4.13.5; 4.22.3; 4.34.1.

**"Vanatam"** — initial-udātta at Rigveda Samhita 1.3.2; 4.4.3; fully unaccented at 1.8.3.

**"Giraḥ"** — this word occurs in some 250 mantras of the Rigveda, meaning "words" or "hymns of praise." It appears in the nominative and accusative plural and the locative singular, always as an initial-udātta word. No further explanation of its meaning is needed.

**Translation:** "Here, continuing the sense of 'Aśvinā': O Ashvins, come — come to this gathering. For what purpose? In answer: Soma-juices have been pressed for your sake, to be drunk — the implied completion being 'in order to accept them.' What kind of pair are the Ashvins? 'Dasrā' — destroyers of enemies; or, as physicians of the gods, destroyers of disease, per the scriptural statement 'the Ashvins are indeed the physicians of the gods' (Aitareya Brahmana 1.18). 'Nāsatyā' — never given to false speech ('asatya'); Yāska himself states in the Nirukta, 'nāsatyā, [those devoted] to truth alone' (Nirukta 6.13). 'Rudravartanī' — whose course resembles the swift charging-path of valiant warriors; or, per a Rigveda citation beginning 'bharatā,' connected with 'vṛkta-barhiṣaḥ' [below]."

*(The grammatical derivation of "dasrā," "yuvākavaḥ," and the accent-rules governing this verse's vocative forms continues in the established dense register; not reproduced in full, consistent with standing practice.)*

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥**

**दस्रा (dasrā)** — destroying enemies, or diseases | **नासत्या (nāsatyā)** — those free of false speech (true to their word) | **रुद्रवर्तनी (rudravartanī)** — those who follow the swift course of valiant warriors (O Ashvin deities!) | **वृक्तबर्हिषः (vṛktabarhiṣaḥ)** — upon the kuśa-grass (barhis), its root cut and laid out | **युवाकवः (yuvākavaḥ)** — mixed with admixtures, or: that which you desire | **सुताः (sutāḥ)** — the Soma, prepared by crushing the creeper, for you to accept | **आ यातम् (ā yātam)** — come here (that is, to the place where we perform this yajna).

### Page 26

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥**

O Ashvin deities! You are destroyers of enemies, or, being physicians of the gods, destroyers of disease. You never speak falsely; you always follow the path of heroes. Being such, come to this, our sacrificial ground, to drink the Soma-juice we have prepared and placed upon the kuśa-grass, the grass fit for the yajna.

**॥ English Translation ॥**

> O Aswins, destroyers of enemies (or of deseases) shorn of untruth, who wander on the path of heroes, come to the mixed libations of Soma juice pressed and placed on lopped Kusa-grass.

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥**

**"Dasrā"** — one of the Ashvin deities is named "Dasra" and the other "Nāsatya"; yet since this word is dual-ending, it designates both together — here, since each name is stated separately, both are correspondingly indicated. **If one holds that these two words function merely as proper names, no further meaning need be constructed for them.** But if one instead regards them as qualifying epithets describing the Ashvins' own qualities, a component-based meaning must be constructed — and this is the course the Bhashyakara himself takes.

**The Bhashyakara explains this word as "śatrūṇām upakṣapayitārau; yadvā deva-vaidyena rogāṇām upakṣapayitārau"** — "destroyers of enemies; or, as physicians of the gods, destroyers of diseases." **Skandasvāmī gives "destroyer of enemies" and also "of beautiful form to behold."** Veṅkaṭamādhava gives "of beautiful form." **Uvvaṭa and Mahīdhara, the commentators on the Vājasaneya Samhita (Shukla Yajurveda), both affirm this same sense for the corresponding word at Yajurveda 13.45.** **Grassmann renders it "Wonder-workers"; Ludwig, "Wonderful"; Monier Williams, "accomplishing wonderful deeds."** All of these scholars, while agreeing broadly on the sense in this particular mantra, render the same word differently in its other occurrences. **Ludwig, for this word in Rigveda Samhita 1.3.1; 1.118.1; 8.8.2, and similar mantras, gives "wonderful"...**

### Page 27

**...at Rigveda Samhita 1.40.12; 8.2.3; 8.3.35; 8.7.1; 8.26.15 and similar, "wonder-workers," those who perform wonderful deeds;**

**at 1.34.3; 1.44.1; 1.47.1; 1.117.15; 8.8.10; 8.8.9; 8.10.1; 8.10.3; 8.10.9 and similar, "beneficent," generous or helpful;**

**at 1.112.14; 1.118.30 and similar, "good-looking," beautiful to behold;**

**at 8.38.1; 8.75.5 and similar, "destroyers" of enemies or disease — various senses given by Ludwig himself across different mantras.** **Geldner similarly offers "master worker, able, dexterous, possessing supernatural strength"; Langlois and Griffith likewise construct differing senses.** **But many hold that, since "dasrā" derives from the root "dṛś" (to see), the sense "worth seeing" or "of beautiful form" is the most fitting one.**

---

**"Yuvākavaḥ"** — Sayanacharya derives this from the root "yu" (to mix), glossing it "mixed." **The "mixture-substances" referred to are cow's milk, curds, barley, and similar admixtures — a topic already treated at length in Volume 1 (pages 675–676).** **Skandasvāmī gives: "yuvāṃ kāmayante iti yuvākavaḥ" — "those who desire to drink you" — meaning "dear to you."** Veṅkaṭamādhava endorses this same sense; **Uvvaṭa and Mahīdhara, commentators on the Vajasaneya Samhita, explain the corresponding word at Yajurveda 13.45 the same way.** Western scholars broadly agree. **Sayanacharya himself, in other mantras — 1.120.2; 1.120.4; 8.5.4; 8.10.3; 8.10.4; 8.10.6 — glosses this same word as "yuvāṃ kāmayamāna," "that which you desire."**

**The word "yuvāka" is used in three places in the Rigveda, but "yuvākavaḥ" occurs only in this one mantra, nowhere else.** A few further examples where "yuvāka" combines with other words in the sense "your" are given below:

- **yuvānīveśyai** (Rigveda Samhita 8.26.3) — **yuvādattasyai** (Rigveda Samhita 8.26.3)
- **yuvāyavaḥ** (Rigveda Samhita 1.15.3) — **yuvāyujaṃ** (Rigveda Samhita 1.118.5)
- **yuvāvate** (Rigveda Samhita 8.19.3)

**In the first two words of this list, the usage carries the same sense as "yuṣmān-ītaḥ"...**

### Page 28

**...at Rigveda Samhita 3.23.1; "yuṣmādattasyai" at 4.46.1; 8.42.6 — these related forms are also well established.**

**"Sutāḥ"** — this word means "pressed out, extracted." When the Soma creeper is crushed with stones (grāvāṇa) and its juice extracted, the Rigveda customarily calls that extracted juice "suta." *(In modern Sanskrit, "suta" instead means "son.")*

**"Nāsatyā"** — a word naming the Ashvin deities; strictly it needs no component-meaning. **Still, the Bhashyakara explains it: "asatyam anṛta-bhāṣaṇaṃ tad-rahitau"** ("free of false speech"), citing two authoritative passages from Yāska: "**satyasyaiva nāsatyā... satyasya pretārau... mitrāgāyaṇa**" **Though different scholars follow different derivational paths for this word, there is unanimity on its meaning.**

**"Vṛktabarhiṣaḥ"** — this word is middle-udātta at Rigveda Samhita 1.3.3; 1.54.4 and similar places; fully unaccented at 1.20.1; 8.2.10; 8.2.13. **Related forms — "vṛktabarhiṣa" at 1.50.2, and "vṛktabarhiṣe" at 1.101.1; 3.56.6; 10.64.15 — also occur. Sayana gives two readings:** "vṛktāni mūlyārjitāni barhīṃṣy āstaraṇa-rūpāṇi yeṣāṃ somānāṃ te vṛktabarhiṣaḥ" — "those Soma-portions whose kuśa-spreads have had their roots cut"; or, following a Rigveda citation beginning "bharatā," read as a nominative in place of an instrumental, meaning "the ritvij who approaches." **That is: on one reading, the kuśa-grass with its root cut, spread out, with the Soma-vessel placed upon it; on the other, "Vṛktabarhiṣa" is one of the eight ritvij-names, and the phrase means "the Soma-juice pressed and prepared by the ritvij of that name."** On the first reading, "Vṛktabarhiṣaḥ" qualifies "Sutāḥ" (the Soma); on the second, it qualifies the ritvij. **Sayana further explains that this kuśa-spread serves to hold the Soma-juice; Skandasvāmī instead explains the kuśa-spread as being for the Ashvins to sit upon when they arrive.** Since, in actual ritual practice, the spreading of barhis is stated in many places as being specifically for holding the oblation-materials or the Soma-juice, **Sayana's view appears the better-supported one.** Though this mantra admits of two readings, Sayana elsewhere consistently glosses this word as **"vṛktabarhiṣa āstaraṇārthaṃ bhinna-darbhāḥ"** — a single, consistent sense, which seems the fitting one. **Among Western scholars: Wilson gives "placed on lopped grass"; Ludwig, "having the barhis cut"; Geldner, "having the Barhis placed around."** In explaining this sense, the words...

### Page 29

**...vary somewhat in exact phrasing but little in overall sense. Grassmann: "of one who has spread the Sacrificial grass"; Monier Williams: "one who has gathered and spread the Sacrificial grass"** — both take this as describing the ritvij who spreads the kusha-grass. **Sayanacharya himself, in other mantras (8.2.1 and similar), confirms this same ritvij-sense for "vṛktabarhiṣaḥ."**

---

**"Rudravartanī"** — this word is fully unaccented at Rigveda Samhita 1.3.3; 8.22.1; 10.61.11, and middle-udātta at 8.22.1:

> आयातं रुद्रवर्तनी । (ऋ. सं. १-३-३)

> युवमश्विना सुपा रुद्रवर्तनी आ सूर्यायै तस्थतुः । (ऋ. सं. १-११८-१?)

> युवमश्विना सुपा रुद्रवर्तनी पुरो रथं कृणुभः शत्वा सख । (ऋ. सं. १०-१९-११?)

> तावित्था ता उषसि शुभस्पती ता यामन्रुद्रवर्तनी । (ऋ. सं. ८-२२-१४?)

**This word occurs only in these four mantras and nowhere else, always as a qualifier of the Ashvins — never of any other deity.** Since it applies only to the Ashvins, whether the Bhashyakara's offered sense truly captures its original meaning remains genuinely uncertain — but since no better-supported alternative is available, his reading must be accepted.

**The Bhashyakara, explaining the word "rudra" itself, gives this derivation:** "so'drodīd ародит tad rudrasya rudratvam" (Taittiriya Samhita 1.8.1) — **"he wept/roared, and hence came the name Rudra" — that is, warriors who make the enemy weep may themselves be called "Rudra."** "Rudravartanī" thus means "those who walk the path of heroes" or "followers of the heroes' path." **Grassmann, following the root "rud" (to shine), glosses "Rudra" as "Brilliant"** — radiant; on this reading, "Rudravartanī" would mean "those who travel on a brilliant, that is, excellent, path." **Alternatively, the Rigveda also knows Rudra as a specific, distinct deity, whose nature — wrathful, slaying and harming enemies — is described in many Rudra-suktas.** This raises the natural question of whether "Rudravartanī" instead means "following the path of that deity Rudra," that is, "destroyers of enemies." **It is therefore not possible to state with certainty which sense this word actually carried at the time.**

### Page 31 — Sūkta 3, Fourth Mantra: Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya

*(Source note: in this scan the Sanskrit bhāṣya is printed in Kannada script. It is rendered below into Devanagari and IAST letter by letter from the page image. Where the print is blurred or looks irregular, the reading is bracketed with [?] rather than corrected from memory.)*

**॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥**

> चित्रभानो चित्रदीप्ते हे इन्द्र अस्मिन्कर्मण्या याहि । आगच्छ । सुता अभिषुता इमे सोमास्त्वायवस्त्वां कामयमाना वर्तन्ते । अण्वीभिः । अग्रुव इत्यादिषु द्वाविंशतिसंख्याकेष्वङ्गुलिनामसु अण्व्य इति पठितम् । ऋत्विजामङ्गुलिभिः सुता इत्यन्वयः । किंच । एते सोमास्तना नित्यं पूतासः पूता शुद्धा दशापवित्रेण बहुधा शोधितत्वात् ।
> *citrabhāno citradīpte he indra asmin karmaṇy ā yāhi | āgaccha | sutā abhiṣutā ime somās tvāyavas tvāṃ kāmayamānā vartante | aṇvībhiḥ | agruva ity ādiṣu dvāviṃśati-saṃkhyākeṣv aṅguli-nāmasu aṇvya iti paṭhitam | ṛtvijām aṅgulibhiḥ sutā ity anvayaḥ | kiṃca | ete somās tanā nityaṃ pūtāsaḥ pūtā śuddhā daśā-pavitreṇa bahudhā śodhitatvāt |*

**Translation:** "'Citrabhāno' — O one of wondrous radiance, O Indra! Come ('yāhi' = 'āgaccha') to this rite. These Soma-juices that are 'sutāḥ' (pressed out) stand here 'tvāyavaḥ' — desiring you. 'Aṇvībhiḥ' — in the list of twenty-two finger-names beginning 'agruvaḥ' (*the Nighaṇṭu list*), 'aṇvyaḥ' is also read; the construction is 'pressed by the fingers of the priests.' Further, these Soma-juices are 'tanā' (continually) 'pūtāsaḥ' — purified, cleansed, since they have been filtered many times through the 'daśā-pavitra' (the woollen cloth with its fringe of threads)."

*(Note: the second "tanā" is taken by the Bhāṣya as "nityam," "constantly"; the sentence "tanā nityaṃ pūtāsaḥ" is read in the print as shown.)*

**The Nirukta's etymologies of "Indra."** The Bhāṣya now cites Yāska (Nirukta 10.8):

> इन्द्रशब्दं यास्को बहुधा निर्वक्ति । इन्द्र इरां दृणातीति वेरां ददातीति वेरां दधातीति वेरां दारयतीति वेरां धारयतीति वेन्दवे द्रवतीति वेन्दौ रमत इति वेन्द्धे भूतानीति वा तद्यदेनं प्राणैः समैन्धंस्तदिन्द्रस्येन्द्रत्वमिति विज्ञायत इदंकरणादित्याग्रायण इदं दर्शनादित्यौपमन्यव इदन्तेर्वैश्वर्यकर्मण इभ्रात्रृणां [?] दारयिता वा द्रावयिता वादरयिता च यज्वनाम् । नि. १०-८ ।
> *indra-śabdaṃ yāsko bahudhā nirvakti | indra irāṃ dṛṇātīti verāṃ dadātīti verāṃ dadhātīti verāṃ dārayatīti verāṃ dhārayatīti vendave dravatīti vendauramata iti vendhe bhūtānīti vā tad yad enaṃ prāṇaiḥ samaindhaṃs tad indrasyendratvam iti vijñāyata idaṃ-karaṇād ity āgrāyaṇa idaṃ darśanād ity aupamanyava idanter vaiśvarya-karmaṇa [?] i[ndraḥ śatrūṇāṃ ?] dārayitā vā drāvayitā vādarayitā ca yajvanām | ni. 10-8 |*

*(Reading note: the print of the clause after "karmaṇa" is blurred, and the letters look like "ibhrātrṛṇām." The Nirukta's own continuation is known to run "indraḥ śatrūṇāṃ dārayitā…", but that is a restoration from outside knowledge, not a clear reading, so it is flagged here. "idanter" is also printed thus, where a form of the root "ind/ind" might be expected. "vera/vendave" etc. are "vā + irām / vā + indave," in sandhi.)*

**Translation:** "Yāska explains the word 'Indra' in many ways: 'Indra' — either because he *tears open* ('dṛṇāti') the 'irā' (food/nourishment); or because he *gives* ('dadāti') irā; or because he *holds/supports* ('dadhāti') irā; or because he *splits* ('dārayati') irā; or because he *sustains* ('dhārayati') irā; or because he *runs* ('dravati') to the 'indu' (Soma-drop); or because he *delights* ('ramate') in the Soma-drop; or because he *kindles* ('indhe') living beings. And it is known (from the Brāhmaṇa) that *'because they kindled him ('samaindhan') with the vital breaths, that is the Indra-hood of Indra.'* Āgrāyaṇa says: 'from "idaṃ-karaṇa," making this (world).' Aupamanyava says: 'from "idaṃ-darśana," seeing this.' [The next clause, drawing on the root 'ind' in the sense of lordship, and the closing sense — Indra as the one who tears apart, drives off, and shatters (the foes) *and* protects the sacrificers — is partly blurred in the print and given here as a paraphrase, not a verified reading.] (Nirukta 10.8)"

> इति । अस्यायमर्थः । दृ विदारण इति धातुः । इरामन्नमुद्दिश्य तन्निष्पादकजलसिद्ध्यर्थं दृणाति मेघं विदीर्णं करोतीतीन्द्रः । डुदाञ् दान इति धातुः । इरामन्नं वृष्टिनिष्पादनेन ददातीतीन्द्रः । धाञ् पोषणार्थः । इरामन्नं तृप्तिकारणं सस्यं दधाति जलप्रदानेन पुष्णातीतीन्द्रः । इरामुत्पादयितुं कर्षकमुखेन भूमिं विदारयतीतीन्द्रः । पूर्वोक्तपोषणमुखेनेरां धारयति विनाशराहित्येन स्थापयतीतीन्द्रः । इन्दुः सोमो वल्लीरसः । तदर्थं यागभूमौ द्रवति धावतीतीन्द्रः । इन्दौ यथोक्ते सोमे रमते क्रीडतीतीन्द्रः । ञिइन्धी दीप्ताविति धातुः । भूतानि प्राणिदेहानिन्द्धे जीवचैतन्यरूपेणान्तः प्रविश्य दीपयतीतीन्द्रः ।
> *iti | asyāyam arthaḥ | dṛ vidāraṇa iti dhātuḥ | irām annam uddiśya tan-niṣpādaka-jala-siddhy-arthaṃ dṛṇāti megham vidīrṇaṃ karotīti indraḥ | ḍudāñ dāna iti dhātuḥ | irām annaṃ vṛṣṭi-niṣpādanena dadātīti indraḥ | dhāñ poṣaṇārthaḥ | irām annaṃ tṛpti-kāraṇaṃ sasyaṃ dadhāti jala-pradānena puṣṇātīti indraḥ | irām utpādayituṃ karṣaka-mukhena bhūmiṃ vidārayatīti indraḥ | pūrvokta-poṣaṇa-mukhenerāṃ dhārayati vināśa-rāhityena sthāpayatīti indraḥ | induḥ somo vallī-rasaḥ | tad-arthaṃ yāga-bhūmau dravati dhāvatīti indraḥ | indau yathokte some ramate krīḍatīti indraḥ | ñi-indhī dīptāv iti dhātuḥ | bhūtāni prāṇi-dehān indhe jīva-caitanya-rūpeṇāntaḥ praviśya dīpayatīti indraḥ |*

**Translation:** "The sense of this is as follows. (1) The root is 'dṛ,' in the sense of splitting: *aiming at irā (food), and for the sake of producing the water that produces it, he splits the cloud open* — hence Indra. (2) The root is 'ḍudāñ,' to give: *he gives irā, food, by bringing rain about* — hence Indra. (3) The root is 'dhāñ,' for nourishing: *he supports irā, food — the grain that is the cause of satiety — nourishing it by the gift of water* — hence Indra. (4) *To bring forth irā he splits the earth, by means of the ploughman* — hence Indra. (5) *By means of the nourishment mentioned above he sustains irā, he establishes it free from destruction* — hence Indra. (6) 'Indu' is the Soma, the juice of the creeper: *for its sake he runs, he hastens, to the ground of the sacrifice* — hence Indra. (7) *He delights, he plays, in the Soma, the 'indu' as described* — hence Indra. (8) The root is 'ñi-indhī,' in the sense of kindling: *he kindles living beings — the bodies of creatures — by entering within them in the form of life-consciousness* — hence Indra."

> एतदेवाभिप्रेत्य वाजसनेयिन आमनन्ति । इन्धो ह वै नाम्येष [?] योऽयं दक्षिणेऽक्षन्पुरुषः । तं वा एतमिन्धं सन्तमिन्द्र इत्याचक्षते । परोक्षेण परोक्षप्रिया इव हि देवाः प्रत्यक्षद्विषः शत. ब्रा. १४-६-१०-२ । इति । तद्यदित्यादिकं ब्राह्मणान्तरवाक्यम् । तत्रेन्द्रविषये निर्वचनमुच्यत इति शेषः ।
> *etad evābhipretya vājasaneyina āmananti | indho ha vai nāmy eṣa [?] yo'yaṃ dakṣiṇe'kṣan puruṣaḥ | taṃ vā etam indhaṃ santam indra ity ācakṣate | parokṣeṇa parokṣa-priyā iva hi devāḥ pratyakṣa-dviṣaḥ | śata. brā. 14-6-10-2 | iti | tad yad ity ādikaṃ brāhmaṇāntara-vākyam | tatra indra-viṣaye nirvacanam ucyata iti śeṣaḥ |*

**Translation:** "With just this in view the Vājasaneyins (the White-Yajurveda school) declare: '*"Indha" indeed is the name of this person who is here in the right eye; and him, though he is "Indha," they call "Indra" — by way of indirect speech; for the gods love the indirect, and are averse to the direct.*' (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 14.6.10.2 [as read in the print]). The sentence beginning 'tad yad…' ('that which…') is from another Brāhmaṇa; the supplied sense is 'in it, an etymology concerning Indra is given.'"

*(Note: "nāmy eṣa" is the print's reading as I could make it out; the sense, 'is the name — this one,' is not affected.)*

> यद्यस्मात्कारणादेनं परमात्मरूपमिन्द्रं देवं प्राणैर्वाक्चक्षुरादीन्द्रियैः प्राणापानादिवायुभिश्च सहितं समैन्धन्नुपासका ध्यानेन सम्यक् प्रकाशितवन्तस्तस्मात्कारणादिन्द्रनाम संपन्नम् — अस्मिन्स्पष्ट [?] इध्यते दीप्यत इति कर्मणि व्युत्पत्तिः । आग्रायणनामको मुनिरिदंकरणादिन्द्र इति निर्वचनं मन्यते । इन्द्रो हि परमात्मरूपेणेदं जगत्करोति । औपमन्यवनामको मुनिरिदंदर्शनादिन्द्र इति निर्वचनमाह । इदमित्यापरोक्ष्यमुच्यते । विवेकेन हि परमात्मानमापरोक्ष्येण पश्यति । एतदेवाभिप्रेत्यारण्यककाण्डे समाम्नायते स एतमेव पुरुषं ब्रह्म ततमम् [?] अपश्यदिदमदर्शमिती३ । तस्मादिदन्द्रो नामेदन्द्रो ह वै नाम तमिदन्द्रं सन्तमिन्द्र इत्याचक्षते परोक्षेण परोक्षप्रिया इव हि देवाः ऐ. आ. २-४-३ । इति । इदि परमैश्वर्य इति धातुः । स्वमायया जगद्रूपत्वं परमैश्वर्यम् । तद्योगादिन्द्रः । अनेनाभिप्रायेण श्रूयते । इन्द्रो…
> *yad yasmāt kāraṇād enaṃ paramātma-rūpam indraṃ devaṃ prāṇair vāk-cakṣur-ādīndriyaiḥ prāṇāpānādi-vāyubhiś ca sahitaṃ samaindhann upāsakā dhyānena samyak prakāśitavantas tasmāt kāraṇād indra-nāma sampannam — asmin-spaṣṭa [?] idhyate dīpyata iti karmaṇi vyutpattiḥ | āgrāyaṇa-nāmako munir idaṃ-karaṇād indra iti nirvacanaṃ manyate | indro hi paramātma-rūpeṇedaṃ jagat karoti | aupamanyava-nāmako munir idaṃ-darśanād indra iti nirvacanam āha | idam ity āparokṣyam ucyate | vivekena hi paramātmānam āparokṣyeṇa paśyati | etad evābhipretyāraṇyaka-kāṇḍe samāmnāyate sa etam eva puruṣaṃ brahma tatamam [?] apaśyad idam adarśam itī3 | tasmād idandro nāmedandro ha vai nāma tam idandraṃ santam indra ity ācakṣate parokṣeṇa parokṣa-priyā iva hi devāḥ | ai. ā. 2-4-3 | iti | idi paramaiśvarya iti dhātuḥ | sva-māyayā jagad-rūpatvaṃ paramaiśvaryam | tad-yogād indraḥ | anenābhiprāyeṇa śrūyate | indro…*

**Translation:** "'Because the worshippers, by meditation, fully kindled this god Indra — whose form is the Supreme Self — together with the senses (vital breaths, speech, sight and the rest) and the vital airs (prāṇa, apāna and the rest), therefore the name "Indra" arose' — in this, the derivation is in the passive: 'in him [?] he is kindled, shines.' The sage named Āgrāyaṇa holds the etymology 'Indra, from *idaṃ-karaṇa* (making this)'; for Indra, in the form of the Supreme Self, makes this world. The sage named Aupamanyava gives the etymology 'Indra, from *idaṃ-darśana* (seeing this)'; 'idam' (this) here denotes direct, immediate vision — for through discrimination one sees the Supreme Self directly. With exactly this in view it is recited in the Āraṇyaka section: '*He beheld this very Person, Brahman, the all-pervading [?]: "I have seen this!"* (— and so on). *Therefore he is "Idandra" by name; "Idandra" indeed is his name; and him, though he is "Idandra," they call "Indra" — by indirect speech; for the gods love the indirect*' (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 2.4.3 [as read in the print]). The root 'idi' means 'supreme lordship'; *the supreme lordship is the becoming-the-world of him by his own māyā; by connection with this he is Indra.* With this intention it is heard: 'Indra…'" *(continues on the next page)*

### Page 32 — Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya concluded; Pada-meanings; Bhāvārtha; English rendering

*(Page header: "Mandala 1, Anuvāka 1, Sūkta 3." Continuing from the previous page, where the Bhāṣya was quoting "indro…".)*

> इन्द्रो मायाभिः पुरुरूप ईयते ऋग्वे. ६-४७-१८ । इति इनशब्दस्येश्वरवाचकस्याकारलोपे सति नकारान्तमिन्निति पदं भवति । द्वृ [?] भये इति धातुः । स च परमेश्वरः शत्रूणां दारयित्वा भीषयितेतीन्द्रः । द्रु गताविति धातुः । शत्रूणां द्रावयित्वा पलायनं प्रापयितेतीन्द्रः । यज्वनां योगानुष्ठायिनामादरयिता भयस्य परिहर्ता । एवमेतानि निर्वचनानि द्रष्टव्यानीति ।
> *indro māyābhiḥ pururūpa īyate | ṛgve. 6-47-18 | iti ina-śabdasyeśvara-vācakasyākāra-lope sati nakārāntam in iti padaṃ bhavati | dṛ [?] bhaye iti dhātuḥ | sa ca parameśvaraḥ śatrūṇāṃ dārayitvā bhīṣayitety indraḥ | dru gatāv iti dhātuḥ | śatrūṇāṃ drāvayitvā palāyanaṃ prāpayitety indraḥ | yajvanāṃ yogānuṣṭhāyinām ādarayitā bhayasya parihartā | evam etāni nirvacanāni draṣṭavyānīti |*

**Translation:** "'*Indra goes forth in many forms by his māyās*' (Ṛgveda 6.47.18). Here the word 'ina,' denoting the Lord, on losing its 'a' becomes the word 'in,' ending in n. (9) The root is 'dṛ [?]' in the sense of fear: *that Supreme Lord, tearing the enemies apart, frightens them* — hence Indra. (10) The root is 'dru,' in the sense of going: *he makes the enemies run, brings them to flight* — hence Indra. (11) *He is the honourer of the sacrificers who practise yoga, and the one who carries them across fear.* In this way these etymologies are to be understood."

*(Reading notes: the Ṛgveda reference is read from the print as "6-47-18"; the print's root-name before "bhaye" is unclear — "dṛ" is my best reading, and the sense is not affected.)*

**॥ Vyākaraṇa notes within the Bhāṣya ॥** *(short; transcribed in full)*

> इन्द्रेत्यत्रामन्त्रिताद्युदात्तत्वम् । आ इत्यत्र निपातत्वेनाद्युदात्तः । चित्रभानो । पदात्परत्वादामन्त्रितनिघातः । त्वामिच्छन्तीत्यर्थे युष्मच्छब्दात्सुप आत्मनः क्यच् । पा. सू. ३-१-८ । प्रत्ययोत्तरपदयोश्च । पा. ७-२-९८ । इति मपर्यन्तस्य त्वादेशः । क्याच्छन्दसि । पा. ३-२-१७० । इति क्यजन्तादुप्रत्ययः । त्वत्य इति प्राप्ते युष्मदस्मदोरनादेशे पा. ७-२-८६ । इत्यविभक्तावपि हलादौ व्यत्ययेनात्त्वम् । उकारः प्रत्ययस्वरेणाद्युदात्तः । अणुशब्दः सौक्ष्म्यवाचकस्तद्योगात्प्रकृतेऽङ्गुलीषु वर्तते । वोतो गुणवचनात् । पा. ४-१-४४ । इति ङीषि प्राप्ते व्यत्ययेन ङीन् । नित्त्वादाद्युदात्तः । तना इत्ययं निपातो नित्यमित्यर्थे निपातत्वादाद्युदात्तः । पूतासः । आज्जसेरसुक् । पा. ७-१-५० । इत्यसुक् ।
> *indretyatrāmantritādyudāttatvam | ā ity atra nipātatvenādyudāttaḥ | citrabhāno | padāt paratvād āmantrita-nighātaḥ | tvām icchantīty arthe yuṣmac-chabdāt sup ātmanaḥ kyac | pā. sū. 3-1-8 | pratyayottarapadayoś ca | pā. 7-2-98 | iti ma-paryantasya tvādeśaḥ | kyāc chandasi | pā. 3-2-170 | iti kyajantād u-pratyayaḥ | tvatya iti prāpte yuṣmadasmador anādeśe pā. 7-2-86 | ity avibhaktāv api halādau vyatyayenātvam | ukāraḥ pratyaya-svareṇādyudāttaḥ | aṇu-śabdaḥ saukṣmya-vācakas tad-yogāt prakṛte 'ṅgulīṣu vartate | voto guṇavacanāt | pā. 4-1-44 | iti ṅīṣi prāpte vyatyayena ṅīn | nittvād ādyudāttaḥ | tanā ity ayaṃ nipāto nityam ity arthe nipātatvād ādyudāttaḥ | pūtāsaḥ | āj-jaser asuk | pā. 7-1-50 | ity asuk |*

**Translation:** "In 'indra' (here a vocative) the first syllable is acute by the vocative rule. 'Ā' is a particle (nipāta), hence acute on its first syllable. 'Citrabhāno' — because it follows another word, the vocative loses its accent (nighāta). 'Tvāyavaḥ' — in the sense 'those who desire you': from the word 'yuṣmad,' the affix 'kyac' after a 'sup'-ending word in the sense of 'one's own wish' (Pāṇini 3.1.8); the substitute 'tva' replaces the stem up to its 'm' (Pāṇini 7.2.98 'pratyayottarapadayoś ca'); then, by 'kyāc chandasi' (Pāṇini 3.2.170), the affix 'u' after a word ending in 'kyac'; where 'tvatya…' would be obtained, the 'a'-substitution takes place by vyatyaya (Vedic licence) even before a non-case-affix beginning with a consonant, per Pā. 7.2.86. The 'u' is acute by the accent of the affix. — 'Aṇvī': the word 'aṇu' denotes fineness; through that association it is applied to the fingers in the present context. Where, by Pā. 4.1.44 ("vāto guṇavacanāt"), the feminine affix ṅīṣ would be expected, 'ṅīn' appears by vyatyaya; since it carries the mark 'n,' the first syllable is acute. 'Tanā' is a particle with the sense 'constantly'; being a particle, first-syllable acute. 'Pūtāsaḥ' — the augment 'asuk' after the 'jas' ending, by Pā. 7.1.50 ('ājjaser asuk')."

*(Reading note, revised at p. 38: at first I read the opening of this sūtra as "voko"; the clearer larger print on p. 38 reads "voto guṇavacanāt" (Pā. 4-1-44), and the text above has been changed to that.)*

**॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥** *(Kannada, translated)*

**चित्रभानो (citrabhāno)** — O Indra, who shine with a wonderful, marvellous radiance | **आ याहि (ā yāhi)** — come (to this sacrificial altar which we are performing) | **त्वायवः (tvāyavaḥ)** — that which you desire (or: which is dear to you) | **इमे सुताः (ime sutāḥ)** — these Soma-juices (those extracted by crushing the Soma creeper) | **अण्वीभिः (aṇvībhiḥ)** — by the fingers (of the priests) (or: by the cloth called the "daśā-pavitra," with which Soma-juice is filtered) | **तना (tanā)** — always | **पूतासः (pūtāsaḥ)** — having been purified, are fit to be drunk.

**॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥** *(Kannada, translated)*

O Indra, who shine with wondrous splendour! The priests have prepared the Soma-juice that is dear to you (or, "for your sake") — filtering it well with their fingers (or with a cloth like a fine net), so that it is fit for drinking. To drink that Soma-juice, may you come to this sacrificial altar of ours.

**English Translation** *(printed in English in the source itself):*

"Come hither, O Indra, of wonderful splendour; these libations of soma juice, ever pure, expressed by the fingers of the priests are deserious [sic — the source's own misprint, evidently for 'desirous'] of you."

**॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥**

This Rik and the following two are an **"aindra-stṛcaḥ"** — that is, a tṛca (triplet) related to Indra: three mantras that praise Indra.

### Page 33 — Kannada commentary: the etymologies of "Indra" (opening)

*(Page header: "Aṣṭaka 1, Adhyāya 1, Varga 5 · Ṛgveda-saṃhitā." From here the page is the Kannada commentary, which re-lists Yāska's and Sāyaṇa's etymologies one by one. The Sanskrit lemmas it quotes repeat what was already transcribed on pp. 31–32 and are given here in short form, in all three layers.)*

**इन्द्र (indra)** — The Bhāṣyakāra, when explaining the derivation of the word "Indra," cites Yāska's Nirukta: "इन्द्र इरां दृणातीति वेरां ददातीति वेरां दधातीति वेरां दारयतीति वेरां धारयतीति वेन्दवे द्रवतीति वेन्दौ रमत इति वेन्द्धे भूतानीति वा तद्यदेनं प्राणैः समैन्धंस्तदिन्द्रस्येन्द्रत्वमिति विज्ञायत इदंकरणादित्याग्रायण इदं दर्शनादित्यौपमन्यव इन्देर्वैश्वर्यकर्मण [?] इभ्रूत्रूणां [?] दारयिता वा द्रावयिता वादरयिता च यज्वनाम् । इति ॥ नि. १०-८ ॥" *(indra irāṃ dṛṇātīti verāṃ dadātīti verāṃ dadhātīti verāṃ dārayatīti verāṃ dhārayatīti vendave dravatīti vendau ramata iti vendhe bhūtānīti vā tad yad enaṃ prāṇaiḥ samaindhaṃs tad indrasyendratvam iti vijñāyata idaṃ-karaṇād ity āgrāyaṇa idaṃ darśanād ity aupamanyava inder vaiśvarya-karmaṇa [?] ibhrūtrūṇāṃ [?] dārayitā vā drāvayitā vādarayitā ca yajvanām | iti || ni. 10-8 ||)* — The commentator himself then gives the sense of this, as follows.

*(Reading note: the same unclear stretch — "…karmaṇa ibhrū-trūṇāṃ…" — appears here as on p. 31, in slightly different letter-forms. Since it recurs in both places, it looks like a printing/ligature problem in the source rather than a one-off blur; I leave it flagged and unrestored.)*

**(1)** *"dṛ vidāraṇe iti dhātuḥ | irām annam uddiśya tan-niṣpādaka-jala-siddhy-arthaṃ dṛṇāti megham vidīrṇaṃ karotīti indraḥ"* (दृ विदारण इति धातुः । इरामन्नमुद्दिश्य तन्निष्पादकजलसिद्ध्यर्थं दृणाति मेघं विदीर्णं करोतीतीन्द्रः) — The root "dṛ" means to tear, to cut. "Irā" means food (āhāra); we obtain it from plants and trees — that is, from the plant kingdom. For that plant kingdom to grow, water is necessary. For the sake of that water — that is, for rain to fall — he cuts open the cloud (with lightning, the thunderbolt-weapon). Because he does so, the name "Indra" arose.

**(2)** *"ḍudāñ dāna iti dhātuḥ | irām annaṃ vṛṣṭi-niṣpādanena dadātīti indraḥ"* (डुदाञ् दान इति धातुः । इरामन्नं वृष्टिनिष्पादनेन ददातीतीन्द्रः) — The root "dā" means to give. "Irā" means food. Because he gives food by means of rain, he is called Indra.

**(3)** *"dhāñ poṣaṇārthaḥ | irām annaṃ tṛpti-kāraṇaṃ sasyaṃ dadhāti jala-pradānena puṣṇātīti indraḥ"* (धाञ् पोषणार्थः । इरामन्नं तृप्तिकारणं सस्यं दधाति जलप्रदानेन पुष्णातीतीन्द्रः) — The root "dhā" means to nourish. Because he nourishes the crops and the like that yield food, by the gift of water (rain), he is called Indra.

**(4)** *"irām utpādayituṃ karṣaka-mukhena bhūmiṃ vidārayatīti indraḥ"* (इरामुत्पादयितुं कर्षकमुखेन भूमिं विदारयतीतीन्द्रः) — For food to be produced, the land must be ploughed. While the land is being ploughed, he makes it split open by the plough and makes it favourable to the crop. Because he does this, he is called Indra.

**(5)** *"pūrvokta-poṣaṇa-mukhenerāṃ dhārayati vināśa-rāhityena sthāpayatīti indraḥ"* (पूर्वोक्तपोषणमुखेनेरां धारयति विनाशराहित्येन स्थापयतीतीन्द्रः) — As said before, having nourished the crops and the like, he becomes their protector, so that they do not perish. Because of this, he is called Indra.

**(6)** *"induḥ somo vallī-rasaḥ | tad-arthaṃ yāga-bhūmau dravati dhāvatīti indraḥ"* (इन्दुः सोमो वल्लीरसः । तदर्थं यागभूमौ द्रवति धावतीतीन्द्रः) — "Indu" means the Soma-juice prepared from the Soma creeper. *(The sentence continues on the next page: for the sake of that Soma, he runs to the sacrificial ground.)*

### Page 34 — Kannada commentary: etymologies of "Indra" (continued)

*(Page header: "Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya-sahitā · Mandala 1, Anuvāka 1, Sūkta 3." Correction note: this page prints the clause "prāṇair vāk-cakṣur-ādīndriyaiḥ" legibly; on p. 31 the first word of that clause was blurred and was provisionally read "pāṇyaiḥ [?]". The p. 31 text has been corrected in place to "prāṇaiḥ," as it is the one reading the clearer print supports.)*

*(Continuation of (6):)* … "Having come, hastening — running swiftly — to such a place, for the sake of drinking the Soma, he is called Indra."

**(7)** *"indau yathokte some ramate krīḍatīti indraḥ"* (इन्दौ यथोक्ते सोमे रमते क्रीडतीतीन्द्रः) — Because he, satisfied by the Soma-juice just described, disports himself in delight, he is called Indra.

**(8)** *"ñi-indhī dīptāv iti dhātuḥ | bhūtāni prāṇi-dehān indhe jīva-caitanya-rūpeṇāntaḥ praviśya dīpayatīti indraḥ"* (ञिइन्धी दीप्ताविति धातुः । भूतानि प्राणिदेहानिन्द्धे जीवचैतन्यरूपेणान्तः प्रविश्य दीपयतीतीन्द्रः) — The root "indh" means to shine, to illumine. Entering the bodies of living beings in the form of consciousness (caitanya), and impelling them to do each of their own deeds, he shines within them; hence he is called Indra.

**(9)** *"yad yasmāt kāraṇād enaṃ paramātma-rūpam indraṃ devaṃ prāṇair vāk-cakṣur-ādīndriyaiḥ prāṇāpānādi-vāyubhiś ca sahitaṃ samaindhann upāsakā dhyānena samyak prakāśitavantas tasmāt kāraṇād indra-nāma sampannam"* (यद्यस्मात्कारणादेनं परमात्मरूपमिन्द्रं देवं प्राणैर्वाक्चक्षुरादीन्द्रियैः प्राणापानादिवायुभिश्च सहितं समैन्धन्नुपासका ध्यानेन सम्यक्प्रकाशितवन्तस्तस्मात्कारणादिन्द्रनाम संपन्नम्) — Because worshippers, in meditation, bring this god — whose form is the Supreme Self — to shine forth well, as joined with the vital breaths, with the senses of speech, sight and the rest, and with the vital airs prāṇa, apāna and the rest, the name "Indra" came about.

**(10)** *"āgrāyaṇa-nāmako munir idaṃ-karaṇād indra iti nirvacanaṃ manyate | indro hi paramātma-rūpeṇedaṃ jagat karoti"* (आग्रायणनामको मुनिरिदंकरणादिन्द्र इति निर्वचनं मन्यते । इन्द्रो हि परमात्मरूपेणेदं जगत्करोति) — "Idaṃ-karaṇa" ("making this") means: in the form of the Supreme Self, Indra creates (brings forth) this world; and so, says the sage named Āgrāyaṇa, this god received the name Indra.

**(11)** *"aupamanyava-nāmako munir idaṃ-darśanād indra iti nirvacanam āha | idam ity āparokṣyam ucyate"* (औपमन्यवनामको मुनिरिदंदर्शनादिन्द्र इति निर्वचनमाह । इदमित्यापरोक्ष्यमुच्यते) — The sage named Aupamanyava says that, because he sees "idam" — that is, everything — the name Indra came about. Here "idam" means "āparokṣya": what is directly present, plain before the eyes (pratyakṣa), as opposed to hidden. *(The commentary adds:)* it is precisely for this reason that the Śruti says "*parokṣa-priyā iva hi devāḥ*" (परोक्षप्रिया इव हि देवाः — "the gods are fond of the indirect, as it were").

**(12)** *"idi paramaiśvarya iti dhātuḥ | sva-māyayā jagad-rūpatvaṃ paramaiśvaryam | tad-yogād indraḥ"* (इदि परमैश्वर्य इति धातुः । स्वमायया जगद्रूपत्वं परमैश्वर्यं । तद्योगादिन्द्रः) — The root "idi" carries the sense "supreme lordship." This god, through his own māyā, has the supreme lordship of taking the form of the world… *(continues on the next page)*

### Page 35 — Etymologies of "Indra" concluded; the word "citrabhānu" begins

*(Correction note: on p. 32 the last etymology's closing word was provisionally read "paripartā"; this page prints it plainly as "parihartā" ("remover of fear"), and p. 32 has been corrected in place.)*

*(Continuation of (12):)* … "…which is the supreme lordship; hence this god is named Indra. This sense is supported by the Vedic sentence '*indro māyābhiḥ pururūpa īyate*' (इन्द्रो मायाभिः पुरुरूप ईयते — 'Indra goes about in many forms by his māyās,' Ṛg. Saṃ. 6-47-18)."

**(13)** *"ina-śabdasyeśvara-vācakasyākāra-lope sati nakārāntam in iti padaṃ bhavati | dṛ bhaye iti dhātuḥ | sa ca parameśvaraḥ śatrūṇāṃ dārayitā bhīṣayitety indraḥ"* (इनशब्दस्येश्वरवाचकस्याकारलोपे सति नकारान्तमिन्निति पदं भवति । दृ भये इति धातुः । स च परमेश्वरः शत्रूणां दारयिता भीषयितेतीन्द्रः) — The word "ina" denotes the Lord. When the "a" following the "n" of this word "ina" is dropped, the form "in" remains. The root *(read here as "dṛ")* means fear. That god, being the Supreme Lord, frightens the enemies; hence his name Indra.

**(14)** *"dru gatāv iti dhātuḥ | śatrūṇāṃ drāvayitā palāyanaṃ prāpayitety indraḥ"* (द्रु गताविति धातुः । शत्रूणां द्रावयिता पलायनं प्रापयितेतीन्द्रः) — The root "dru" means going — that is, to go, to run away. This god makes enemies flee; hence he is named Indra.

**(15)** *"yajvanāṃ yogānuṣṭhāyināṃ ādarayitā bhayasya parihartā"* (यज्वनां योगानुष्ठायिनामादरयिता भयस्य परिहर्ता) — Because he honours those who worship him with sacrifices and the like (and who practise yoga), and removes their fear, this god is named Indra.

In just this fashion many more etymologies of the word "Indra" may be devised.

**चित्रभानो (citrabhāno)** — The Bhāṣyakāra, Skandasvāmī, Veṅkaṭamādhava and the Western scholars as well all explain this word as "one who shines with a wondrous (vicitra) or astonishing radiance." There is no notable difference of opinion among them. The word "citrabhānu" is used with reference to the deities **Agni, Indra, Savitṛ and the Maruts**. The Ṛks containing the word are given below.

> चित्रभानुरुषसां भात्यग्रेऽपां गर्भः प्रस्व१ आ विवेश । (ऋ. सं. ७-९-३ [?])
